paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: However, the results seem to focus on LLMs only.

analysis.core_claim: The weakness is reliable because the paper’s experimental section is primarily an evaluation of different LLM architectures, sizes, and pretraining regimes, with only limited comparison to non-LLM or HTML-structure-specific models. The reviewer’s wording is somewhat broad, since the paper does include a few external baselines, but the main results and analysis do focus on LLM variants.
paper_evidence: The paper explicitly frames the study around LLMs: it evaluates “a variety of pretrained LLMs,” varying architecture, size, and training data, and asks whether off-the-shelf LLMs can transfer to HTML understanding.

Section 7 lists the main models as Transformer LLM families: T5, LaMDA, PaLM, BERT, MobileBERT, and ALBERT. The comparisons are mostly between encoder-decoder, decoder-only, and encoder-only language models, plus versions trained from scratch.

Section 8 says it evaluates “HTML pre-trained encoder-decoder architectures,” compares against “other LLM architectures and training regimes,” and then has subsections on pretraining effect, architecture effect, and model-size effects—all centered on LLM variants.

For Semantic Classification, the paper compares T5 variants, BERT-style models, LaMDA, PaLM, and models trained from scratch. It does not compare against HTML/tree-aware models such as StructuralLM, MarkupLM, or the specialized architectures mentioned in related work.

For Description Generation, the main comparisons are WebD-T5 and decoder-only LLMs, plus a simple heuristic baseline, “Closest Description.” This supports the reviewer’s point that the results are not broadly benchmarked against task-specific HTML models.

For Autonomous Web Navigation, the paper does include non-LLM prior baselines such as CC-Net and WGE on MiniWoB. This means the statement is not literally true for every result, but the overall experimental focus remains LLM-centered.

The review context clarifies the concern: the reviewer wants to know whether practitioners should use an HTML-specific model trained on small data or fine-tune an LLM. The paper’s comparisons do not fully answer that because many HTML-specific or structure-aware alternatives are absent.
analysis.reasoning: The target segment says, “However, the results seem to focus on LLMs only.” This is grounded in the paper. The paper’s main contribution is empirical: fine-tuning and analyzing LLMs for HTML understanding. Most of the experimental design varies LLM architecture, pretraining, size, and data amount. The paper does compare to prior supervised web-navigation models on MiniWoB and uses a heuristic baseline for description generation, so the phrase “LLMs only” would be too strong if read literally. However, the reviewer says “seem to focus,” which is a softer and accurate characterization of the dominant emphasis. In the broader review, this weakness is used to argue that the paper does not sufficiently compare fine-tuned LLMs against HTML-specific or tree-structured models. That criticism is supported by the paper: despite claiming that LLMs can avoid specialized architectures, the semantic classification and description generation sections largely compare LLMs against other LLMs or simple baselines rather than against strong task-specific HTML-understanding systems.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness claiming that a paper’s results “focus mostly on X models/methods” is reliable when the experimental section primarily varies models within that family—e.g., architecture, size, pretraining, or fine-tuning of X—and lacks strong comparisons to the alternative family needed to support the paper’s broader claim. The weakness can remain reliable even if the paper includes a few external or heuristic baselines, as long as those baselines are limited to some tasks, are not the main focus of the analysis, or do not include the most relevant competing task-specific methods.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark such a weakness unreliable merely because the paper has one or two non-X baselines; check whether the central results and conclusions are still mostly intra-family comparisons.

Check whether the paper makes a broad practical claim, such as replacing specialized architectures. If so, absence of strong specialized baselines makes a “focuses mostly on LLMs” criticism more reliable.

Distinguish between literal overstatement and fair characterization. “Only” may be imperfect, but phrases like “seem to focus” can be reliable when the dominant experimental emphasis matches the criticism.
Look task by task: a paper may compare against prior work on one benchmark but still lack relevant baselines on other core tasks.
A weakness is stronger when the reviewer names plausible omitted baselines or categories of baselines that are directly relevant to the paper’s claims.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: I expect to see more task-specific models such as StructuralLM [1], MarkupLM [2] that respect the tree structure of HTML (or some other methods mentioned in the paper) to be evaluated against.

analysis.core_claim: The weakness is reliable because the paper makes broad claims that fine-tuned general LLMs are preferable to specialized HTML-understanding architectures, but its experimental comparisons do not consistently include strong HTML/tree/markup-aware task-specific models across the proposed tasks.
paper_evidence: The abstract explicitly frames the contribution against prior specialized approaches: “previous work has developed dedicated architectures and training procedures for HTML understanding,” and claims that LLMs transfer well to HTML understanding tasks.

The introduction says the paper investigates whether LLMs can produce better-performing, more sample-efficient HTML understanding models “without the need for custom NN architecture design.” This makes comparison to custom/tree-aware architectures central to the paper’s claim.
For Autonomous Web Navigation, the paper does compare against specialized prior systems such as CC-Net and WGE on MiniWoB, so the reviewer’s criticism is not equally applicable to every task.

For Semantic Classification, the comparisons are mostly among LLM variants, BERT-style encoders, decoder-only models, T5 models, and models trained from scratch on the task data. The paper does not evaluate strong markup/tree-aware pretrained models such as MarkupLM, StructuralLM, or comparable HTML-specific architectures.
For Description Generation, the main non-LLM baseline is a heuristic “Closest Description” baseline. There is no comparison to task-specific or structure-aware HTML/document understanding models.

The paper’s preprocessing section uses snippet extraction from the HTML tree, but the model inputs are then unparsed raw text. Since the paper argues this raw-text LLM approach can avoid specialized HTML architectures, it is reasonable to ask for direct comparison against models that exploit HTML/tree structure.

The related work section itself emphasizes that many prior web/HTML systems rely on specialized neural architectures or HTML preprocessing, but the experimental section does not systematically benchmark against such methods on all three tasks.
analysis.reasoning: The target segment is grounded in a real gap between the paper’s claims and its evidence. The paper is not merely presenting an internal ablation of LLM architectures; it repeatedly positions fine-tuned LLMs as an alternative to dedicated HTML-understanding models and claims sample-efficiency/performance advantages over specialized approaches. Given that framing, it is reasonable for a reviewer to expect comparisons against HTML-specific or markup/tree-aware models. The paper partially satisfies this for MiniWoB by comparing against CC-Net and WGE, but the other two tasks—especially Semantic Classification and Description Generation—mainly compare T5/LaMDA/PaLM/BERT variants, scratch training, and a simple heuristic. That leaves the central practical question under-tested: whether one should fine-tune a generic LLM or use a model designed/pretrained for structured markup or document layout. The named examples, StructuralLM and MarkupLM, may not be perfect drop-in baselines for every task, but they are plausible representatives of structure-aware/task-specific document or markup models, and the reviewer also allows “some other methods mentioned in the paper.” Therefore the criticism is concrete, tied to the paper’s stated motivation, and supported by omissions in the experimental design.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness asking for additional baselines is reliable when the paper’s main claims are comparative—e.g., claiming to outperform, replace, or avoid specialized methods—but the experiments compare mostly within the authors’ preferred model family or only against weak/partial baselines. Check whether the missing baselines are relevant to the claimed advantage and whether the paper itself cites or motivates that class of methods. The criticism remains reliable even if the paper has some baselines, if those baselines cover only one task or do not test the central comparison across the paper’s main settings.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark this kind of criticism reliable if the requested baselines are unrelated to the task, incompatible with the input/output setting, or impossible to adapt without changing the problem definition.
Do not require every named model literally if the broader baseline class is already well represented by strong, comparable systems across all key tasks.
Be cautious when a paper’s contribution is explicitly exploratory or diagnostic rather than claiming superiority over specialized systems; then missing SOTA baselines may be a weaker criticism.
A baseline criticism is stronger when the paper itself cites the missing family of methods or frames its contribution as avoiding/replacing that family.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: Models that are trained on task specific data to compare against is questionable.

analysis.core_claim: The weakness is reliable because the paper makes broad comparative claims about LLMs replacing or outperforming task-specific/specialized HTML-understanding models, but much of the experimental comparison is against other LLM variants, models trained from scratch, or limited baselines rather than strong task-specific HTML/markup-aware models across all tasks.
paper_evidence: The abstract claims that fine-tuned LLMs are “12% more accurate at semantic classification compared to models trained exclusively on the task dataset” and that they complete MiniWoB tasks with “192x less data compared to the previous best supervised model.” This makes the choice of comparison models central to the paper’s contribution.

The introduction explicitly contrasts the paper’s approach with “specialized models” that use HTML structural inductive biases, citing Liu et al. (2018), Toyama et al. (2021), Gur et al. (2021), and Humphreys et al. (2022), and claims that pretrained LLMs can avoid “the need for custom NN architecture design.”

For autonomous web navigation, the paper does compare against prior specialized MiniWoB systems such as CC-Net and WGE. This partially addresses the concern, but only for one of the three tasks and only on the subset of 48 MiniWoB websites common across models.

For semantic classification, the experiments mainly compare T5, BERT-style encoders, LaMDA, PaLM, and versions trained from scratch on the task data. These are mostly general Transformer/LLM baselines, not strong HTML-specific or markup-structure-aware systems.

For description generation, the main non-LLM baseline is “Closest Description,” an intuitive heuristic. The paper does not compare against learned task-specific models that exploit DOM/tree structure or markup-aware pretraining.
Section 8.4 frames conclusions around pretraining, architecture, and model size, again focusing on LLM variants and training regimes rather than a broad comparison to task-specific HTML models.

The reviewer’s surrounding comments clarify the target weakness: they expected comparisons to HTML/structure-aware models such as StructuralLM or MarkupLM, or other methods mentioned by the paper, and they argue that the paper’s setup does not fully answer whether practitioners should use an HTML-specific model trained on a small dataset or fine-tune an LLM.
analysis.reasoning: The criticism is grounded in a mismatch between the paper’s claims and its evidence. The paper is not merely studying LLM variants in isolation; it repeatedly positions fine-tuned LLMs as an alternative to specialized HTML-understanding architectures and task-specific training pipelines. Therefore, it is reasonable for a reviewer to question whether the comparison set is sufficient. Although the paper includes meaningful prior baselines for MiniWoB, the other two tasks rely heavily on comparisons among pretrained LLMs, encoder/decoder variants, from-scratch Transformers, and a heuristic baseline. That does not fully establish superiority over strong task-specific or markup-aware models. The weakness is also appropriately phrased as “questionable” rather than claiming the paper has no baselines at all. The paper does have baselines, but given the main framing, the reviewer’s concern that the chosen task-specific comparisons are incomplete is supported by the experimental design.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness about questionable comparison models is reliable when the paper makes claims about outperforming or replacing a class of methods, but the experiments either omit strong representatives of that class, include them only for some tasks, or mostly compare against variants of the authors’ preferred model family. To judge this, check whether the paper’s abstract/introduction/conclusion frame the contribution as superior to specialized or task-specific models, then verify whether the experiments actually include strong, relevant baselines for each major task. If the baselines are mostly ablations, from-scratch versions, heuristics, or models from the same family, the weakness is grounded even if some baselines are present.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark such a criticism unreliable merely because the paper has some baselines; ask whether those baselines support the specific comparative claim being made.
A comparison concern is especially credible when the paper’s headline claims mention prior best supervised models, specialized architectures, or reduced need for task-specific models.
If only one task has strong prior baselines while other tasks use weak heuristics or same-family variants, a reviewer can reliably criticize the overall comparison setup.

The criticism is less reliable if the suggested baselines are clearly inapplicable to the task or unavailable under comparable inputs, but here the broader concern remains valid because the paper itself emphasizes HTML/structure-aware alternatives.
When a paper’s main result is empirical rather than methodological, baseline choice is a core quality issue, not a minor preference.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: One key question not answered in this context is how much of HTML structure analysis and understanding is truly required for these questions.

analysis.core_claim: The weakness is reliable because the paper repeatedly frames its contribution as “HTML understanding” requiring structure/content understanding, but its experiments mainly show that fine-tuned LLMs perform well on selected tasks; they do not isolate whether success depends on genuine HTML structural reasoning versus surface/local textual cues such as nearby labels, attributes, ids, or action histories.
paper_evidence: The paper explicitly claims the benchmark tasks “capture the essence” of HTML understanding and “require understanding both structure and content.” This makes the reviewer’s question directly relevant to the paper’s stated premise.

For Semantic Classification, the paper’s own example says the model can use the input attributes `type="email"` and `id="uName"`, the label text, and neighboring elements. These are partly local lexical/attribute cues, so the paper itself leaves open how much tree-structural reasoning is necessary.

For Description Generation, the dataset is auto-labeled using the HTML `label` element’s `for` attribute matching the target element’s `id`. Although the authors replace some label tags to avoid trivial cheating, the task may still often be solvable by locating nearby or associated text rather than demonstrating broad structural page understanding.

For Autonomous Web Navigation, MiniWoB pages are simulated and generally small enough that the paper keeps full HTML pages rather than dealing with large real-world pages. This limits evidence about whether models understand realistic HTML structure.

The experiments compare pretrained vs non-pretrained models, architectures, model sizes, action-history ablations, and snippet-size settings. They do not include a direct structural-ablation experiment such as removing/replacing tags, shuffling DOM order, masking attributes, removing ids/classes, or comparing against strong non-structural lexical baselines across all tasks.
The paper itself offers only a hypothesis that T5’s bidirectional attention may help recover information lost when tree-structured HTML is linearized; it does not directly test this hypothesis.

The appendix error analysis says 32% of Semantic Classification errors are due to lack of information in snippets, suggesting snippet extraction/available context matters, but this still does not quantify how much actual HTML structure analysis is required.
analysis.reasoning: The target segment does not deny the paper’s empirical results; it questions an unisolated causal interpretation behind them. That is a grounded weakness. The paper’s central framing is that LLMs can perform HTML understanding, and it states that the chosen tasks require structural and content understanding. However, the reported experiments primarily evaluate end-task accuracy/success and compare model families. They do not systematically separate structural reasoning from simpler cues. For example, Semantic Classification may be driven by values like `type`, `id`, placeholder text, or nearby labels; Description Generation is based on recovering label text associated through HTML conventions; and MiniWoB navigation uses small synthetic pages with reference selectors and action histories. The reviewer’s broader context also proposes a concrete structural-control experiment: replacing non-salient HTML tags with a dummy token. That kind of experiment is absent from the paper. Therefore, the target weakness is well supported: the paper shows LLMs work on these tasks, but does not answer how much HTML structure understanding is truly needed for that performance.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness is reliable when a paper claims that a model performs a high-level capability such as “understanding structure,” but the experiments only measure task performance and do not include controls that rule out simpler lexical, local, annotation, or dataset-specific shortcuts. To judge reliability, check whether the paper directly tests the claimed mechanism with ablations such as masking attributes/text, removing or corrupting structural tags, shuffling tree order, comparing to bag-of-tokens or nearest-text baselines, evaluating on structure-heavy examples, or using adversarial examples where surface cues fail. If such tests are missing and the tasks plausibly admit shortcut solutions, then a reviewer’s concern that the required structural understanding is unproven is grounded and reliable.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark this type of weakness unreliable merely because the paper reports strong accuracy; strong task performance does not by itself establish the claimed kind of reasoning.
The weakness is especially reliable when the paper uses terms like “understanding,” “structure,” or “semantics” but evaluates only downstream outcomes.
Look for whether the paper’s own examples reveal local attributes, labels, ids, or text that could solve many instances without global structure reasoning.
Check whether any baselines actually test the shortcut hypothesis. A generic model comparison, size ablation, or pretraining ablation is not the same as a structural-ablation test.

A weakness would be less reliable if the paper already included adversarial structural evaluations, tag/tree masking studies, DOM-order perturbations, or examples designed so local lexical cues are insufficient.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: The novelty is primarily empirical, and the technical approach is essentially an application of known techniques (the standard pretrain-finetune paradigm of LLMs).

analysis.core_claim: The weakness is reliable because the paper’s main contribution is an empirical study/benchmarking of existing pretrained LLM architectures on HTML-understanding tasks, using the standard fine-tuning paradigm, rather than proposing a substantially new model architecture, learning algorithm, or technical method.
paper_evidence: The abstract frames the contribution as “HTML understanding models (fine-tuned LLMs) and an in-depth analysis” across three tasks, not as a new architecture or training objective.

The introduction explicitly says the paper investigates whether off-the-shelf LLMs can be applied to HTML understanding “without the need for custom NN architecture design.” This supports the reviewer’s claim that the technical approach is applying known LLM methods rather than inventing new ones.

The paper’s central setup is to evaluate existing Transformer LLM families—T5, LaMDA, PaLM, BERT/MobileBERT/ALBERT—varying architecture, size, and pretraining corpora. These are all known model classes rather than newly proposed architectures.

Section 7, “Model Training,” describes standard fine-tuning: encoder-decoder and decoder-only models receive text input and text output; encoder-only models add a classification head. This is the standard pretrain-then-finetune recipe.

The paper repeatedly emphasizes empirical findings: pretrained LLMs transfer well to HTML tasks, T5 performs best, model size has diminishing returns, context window is a bottleneck, and labeled data requirements are reduced. These are evaluation/analysis conclusions rather than new technical mechanisms.

The preprocessing contribution is relatively lightweight: raw HTML is serialized as text, with snippet extraction around salient elements for long pages. This is a practical input-processing heuristic, not enough to make the paper technically novel in the sense of a new modeling method.

The paper’s claimed contributions include a suite of tasks, evaluation across architectures, and an open-source CommonCrawl-derived description-generation dataset. These are valuable empirical/resource contributions, consistent with the reviewer’s wording that the novelty is “primarily empirical.”

The review context itself is consistent: the reviewer praises the paper’s comprehensive evaluations and new dataset/benchmark, but says the technical approach lacks novelty. This matches the paper’s actual contribution profile.
analysis.reasoning: The target weakness does not misrepresent the paper. The paper’s own motivation is to avoid specialized neural architectures and instead test whether pretrained LLMs can be used directly on raw HTML. Its experimental sections focus on fine-tuning existing LLMs on three tasks and comparing architectures, data sizes, and baselines. The strongest claims are empirical: improved sample efficiency on MiniWoB, better semantic classification accuracy, strong description generation performance, T5 outperforming other architectures, and diminishing returns from scale. Although the paper has novelty in task framing, dataset construction, and empirical analysis, the reviewer carefully qualifies the criticism as “primarily empirical,” not “no novelty.” That distinction makes the weakness well-grounded. A less reliable version would claim the paper has no contribution at all, but this segment specifically targets technical novelty and correctly identifies the method as the standard LLM pretrain-finetune paradigm.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness claiming “limited technical novelty; mostly empirical application of known pretrain/fine-tune methods” is reliable when the paper mainly evaluates existing pretrained models or standard architectures on a new domain/task, uses ordinary fine-tuning or prompting with minimal methodological changes, and presents its contributions as benchmarks, datasets, comparisons, ablations, or empirical findings. It remains reliable even if the paper has valuable empirical/resource novelty, as long as the criticism is specifically about lack of new modeling/training technique rather than denying all contribution.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark such a weakness reliable if the paper actually introduces a new architecture, objective, inference algorithm, data-generation method central to performance, or theoretical framework that the reviewer ignores.

Be careful if the review says “no novelty” while the paper clearly contributes a new benchmark/dataset; that may be too broad. The present segment is reliable because it says novelty is “primarily empirical,” which allows for dataset and analysis contributions.
Check whether the paper’s method section contains only standard fine-tuning/prompting of known models plus routine preprocessing; if so, the weakness is usually grounded.
Check whether the paper’s own contribution statements emphasize empirical evaluation, resource release, or analysis rather than a new technical mechanism.
A preprocessing heuristic alone should not be treated as major technical novelty unless the paper shows it is a central methodological contribution with substantial new design and evidence.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: Basically, I need to see the following question answered: "For specific web tasks, do I want to use a HTML specific model trained on the small dataset or just to fine-tune LLMs"?

analysis.core_claim: The reviewer’s weakness is reliable because the paper’s central practical claim is that fine-tuned general LLMs can replace or outperform specialized HTML/web-task models, but the experiments do not consistently provide controlled comparisons against HTML-specific or structure-aware models trained under comparable small-data conditions.
paper_evidence: The introduction explicitly frames the work against specialized HTML/web automation models: prior work uses “specialized models,” “application-specific datasets,” and “neural network architectures to leverage inductive biases of the HTML’s structure,” while this paper proposes using off-the-shelf LLMs on raw HTML instead.

The paper claims that pretrained LLMs can achieve strong HTML understanding “without the need for custom NN architecture design” and that they are more sample-efficient than models trained from scratch.

For autonomous web navigation, the paper compares WebN-T5 models to CC-Net and WGE on MiniWoB, but the key comparison is not controlled for data size: WebN-T5 uses 12K public demonstrations, while CC-Net supervised is described as using 2.4M demonstrations. This supports a sample-efficiency claim, but does not fully answer whether a specialized HTML model trained on the same small dataset would be preferable.

For semantic classification, the paper compares T5 variants, BERT-style encoders, LaMDA/PaLM, and models trained from scratch. However, these are mostly generic Transformer/LLM variants, not clearly HTML-specific models with structural inductive bias such as tree-aware or markup-pretrained systems.
For description generation, the paper introduces a CommonCrawl-derived dataset and compares LLMs to a simple “Closest Description” heuristic baseline, but not to specialized HTML/markup models.

The review context makes the same point in neighboring sentences: the reviewer asks for task-specific models such as StructuralLM or MarkupLM and says the results “seem to focus on LLMs only.” The target sentence summarizes that missing practical comparison.
analysis.reasoning: The target weakness is grounded in the mismatch between the paper’s stated motivation and its experimental coverage. The paper wants to persuade practitioners that, for HTML understanding and web automation, they can fine-tune general pretrained LLMs on raw HTML instead of designing or training specialized HTML-aware models. To substantiate that practical recommendation, the most relevant experiment would compare fine-tuned LLMs against HTML-specific or structure-aware models under similar task data budgets. The paper partially addresses this for MiniWoB by comparing to prior specialized web-navigation systems, but those baselines are not matched in training data and are only one of the three tasks. For semantic classification and description generation, the comparisons are mainly among LLM architectures, pretrained versus non-pretrained versions, encoder/decoder variants, and a simple heuristic baseline. Therefore, the reviewer’s requested question—whether to use an HTML-specific model trained on the small dataset or just fine-tune an LLM—is a legitimate missing comparison, not an unsupported complaint. The segment is especially reliable because it targets the evidentiary support for the paper’s main claim rather than asking for an unrelated extension.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness is reliable when it identifies a missing baseline that is necessary to validate the paper’s own central comparative claim. If a paper argues that a new general-purpose approach removes the need for specialized/task-specific models, then the experiments should include controlled comparisons to those specialized models, preferably under comparable data and evaluation settings. If the paper instead compares mostly variants of its own model family, simple heuristics, or prior systems with very different data budgets, a reviewer is justified in saying the main practical question remains unanswered.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Check whether the paper’s abstract/introduction makes a practitioner-facing claim such as “no need for specialized architectures” or “better than task-specific models.” Such claims raise the bar for specialized-model baselines.
A baseline comparison is weaker evidence if the competing model was trained with a very different amount of data, evaluated on only a subset of tasks, or taken from a different experimental protocol.

Comparing pretrained versus non-pretrained versions of the same general architecture does not substitute for comparing to genuinely task-specific or structure-aware models when the paper’s claim is about replacing those models.
A reviewer’s missing-baseline criticism is more reliable when neighboring review text names plausible omitted model classes and explains why they are relevant to the paper’s claim.

The criticism would be less reliable if the requested baselines were clearly outside the paper’s task scope, unavailable/inapplicable to the input-output format, or already included under matched settings.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: I don't see the point of compare different variants of LLMs with or without pre-training.

analysis.core_claim: The weakness is reliable because the paper’s main motivation is to show that fine-tuned pretrained LLMs are preferable to task-specific or HTML-specific approaches, but much of the experimental comparison is instead among LLM variants, including pretrained vs. non-pretrained versions. Those ablations are useful internally, but they do not fully answer the practical baseline question raised by the reviewer: whether one should use an HTML/task-specific model or fine-tune a general LLM.
paper_evidence: The paper frames its motivation around replacing specialized HTML/web models: it says prior work uses “specialized models” and “custom NN architecture design,” and the paper aims to test whether LLMs can produce better, more sample-efficient HTML understanding models “without the need for custom NN architecture design.”

The abstract makes comparative claims against non-LLM/task-specific approaches, e.g. “fine-tuned LLMs are 12% more accurate at semantic classification compared to models trained exclusively on the task dataset” and “complete 50% more tasks using 192x less data compared to the previous best supervised model.”

However, in the Semantic Classification section, the main comparisons are among WebC-T5, WebC-BERT, WebC-LaMDA, WebC-PaLM, and versions trained from scratch. These are mostly LLM/Transformer-family comparisons rather than comparisons to strong HTML- or document-structure-specific models such as MarkupLM/StructuralLM or other specialized HTML architectures.

In Description Generation, the dataset is newly constructed, so the paper mainly compares LLM variants plus a simple “Closest Description” heuristic baseline. This supports internal LLM analysis but not a broad claim that LLMs are better than HTML-specific systems.

The paper explicitly devotes Section 8.4 to “Pre-training Effect” and “Architecture Effect,” concluding that pretraining matters and T5 performs best. This shows why the authors included pretrained vs. non-pretrained LLM comparisons, but it also confirms the reviewer’s point that a substantial part of the evaluation is focused on LLM-internal ablations rather than the reviewer’s desired practical comparison.

The complete review context clarifies the target sentence: the reviewer’s preceding complaint is that comparisons to task-specific models are questionable and that stronger HTML/tree-aware models should be evaluated. The following sentence states the desired question: “For specific web tasks, do I want to use a HTML specific model trained on the small dataset or just to fine-tune LLMs?”
analysis.reasoning: The target sentence is somewhat colloquial—“I don’t see the point”—but in context it is not an unsupported dismissal. The reviewer is identifying a mismatch between the paper’s broad positioning and its evidence. The paper claims practical significance from using pretrained LLMs instead of specialized HTML architectures, yet many experiments isolate differences among LLM architectures, sizes, and pretraining regimes. Those comparisons are scientifically meaningful for understanding LLM behavior, and the paper does provide a rationale for them in Section 8.4. However, they do not by themselves establish that practitioners should prefer fine-tuned general LLMs over strong HTML-specific or structure-aware models. Thus the weakness is grounded in the paper’s actual experimental scope: the paper answers “which LLM/pretraining setup works best?” more thoroughly than “is a general pretrained LLM better than a purpose-built HTML model?” Because the review segment is part of a broader baseline-comparison criticism, it should be treated as reliable.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness is reliable when it points out that a paper’s ablation studies or model-variant comparisons do not match the paper’s main comparative claim. If a paper argues that method family A is preferable to task-specific/specialized alternatives, but mostly compares variants within family A or compares only to weak/non-representative baselines, then a reviewer can reliably criticize those comparisons as insufficiently motivated or insufficient for the main claim—even if the internal ablations are themselves technically valid.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark this kind of weakness unreliable merely because the paper includes some explanation for the ablation; the issue may be whether the ablation answers the central claim.
Check the surrounding review context. A vague sentence like “I don’t see the point” may be reliable if adjacent sentences specify the missing comparison or practical question.

Look for mismatch between paper motivation and evidence: claims about replacing specialized models require strong specialized baselines, not only pretrained-vs-scratch variants of the proposed model family.
Distinguish internal scientific value from claim support. Pretraining ablations can be useful while still being insufficient for the paper’s broader practical positioning.
For new datasets, simple heuristic baselines may be understandable, but broad claims about superiority over existing task-specific models still need careful qualification.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: I examined the supplementary material provided by the authors and only found the data files.

analysis.core_claim: The supplementary material appears to provide data artifacts but not code, which limits reproducibility of the reported experiments.
paper_evidence: The paper repeatedly frames its released artifact as a dataset, not code: the abstract says the authors “create and open-source a large-scale HTML dataset distilled and auto-labeled from CommonCrawl.”

In the introduction, the authors say: “To encourage further research in this direction, we plan to open-source our dataset for description generation.” This is a dataset-release promise, with no corresponding promise to release training/evaluation code.

In Section 5 on Description Generation, the paper states: “A small sample is available in the supplemental material, while the entire dataset will be available upon publication.” This directly supports the reviewer’s observation that the supplementary material contains data files.

Appendix A.1 gives dataset construction details and again focuses on the dataset contents and preprocessing choices. It does not describe an accompanying codebase or scripts for reproducing the experiments.

The paper contains many implementation-sensitive components—snippet extraction, MiniWoB action formatting, fine-tuning multiple LLM families, action-history augmentation, and evaluation over selected MiniWoB tasks—but the provided text does not indicate that code for these components is included in the supplement.

The review context later repeats the same reproducibility concern: “The Supplementary Material only provides the data file” and “It is better to make the codes available for reproducing these results,” showing that the target sentence is part of a concrete reproducibility criticism rather than an isolated unsupported complaint.
analysis.reasoning: The target segment is reliable because it is consistent with what the paper itself claims to release. The authors emphasize dataset creation and say that a sample of the dataset is in the supplementary material, while the full dataset will be available upon publication. Nowhere in the paper text do they claim to provide source code, training scripts, evaluation scripts, model checkpoints, or MiniWoB reproduction code. Since the results depend on nontrivial engineering choices—HTML snippet extraction, action-history formatting, model fine-tuning across T5/LaMDA/PaLM/BERT variants, and benchmark-specific evaluation—the absence of code is a meaningful reproducibility issue. The reviewer’s statement does not mischaracterize the paper’s scientific contribution; it specifically comments on the contents of the supplementary material and is aligned with the paper’s own artifact description, which focuses on data rather than code.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness about supplementary material being limited to data files is reliable when the paper’s artifact claims mention only datasets/samples and do not state that code, scripts, checkpoints, or full reproduction instructions are provided—especially if the experiments require substantial implementation details beyond the written description. Treat such a weakness as grounded if the paper itself emphasizes dataset release but is silent about code release.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark this type of weakness reliable if the paper explicitly provides a public code repository, scripts, or reproducibility package and the reviewer ignores it.
Be cautious if the reviewer claims to have inspected supplementary files but the paper text clearly lists code artifacts in the supplement; then the criticism may be contradicted by the paper.
A missing-code criticism is stronger when the experiments involve complex preprocessing, model training, or benchmark evaluation that cannot be trivially reconstructed from the paper alone.

A statement that the supplement contains only data is less reliable if the review gives no connection to reproducibility and the paper’s contribution is purely a dataset paper where code is not necessary.
Check whether the paper promises code release upon publication; if so, the review should distinguish between ‘not currently in supplement’ and ‘will never be released.’

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: It would be better if there were codes to prove its reproducibility.

analysis.core_claim: The reviewer’s weakness is that the paper would be more reproducible if it released code, and this is grounded because the paper emphasizes empirical results across many models/tasks but only promises or provides data, not implementation code sufficient to reproduce the experiments.
paper_evidence: The paper’s main contributions are heavily empirical: it fine-tunes and compares many LLMs across three tasks—Semantic Classification, Description Generation, and Autonomous Web Navigation—and reports claims such as up to 192× sample efficiency and T5 models performing best across tasks.

For the new Description Generation dataset, the paper says: “To encourage further research in this direction, we plan to open-source our dataset for description generation,” and later: “the entire dataset will be available upon publication.” This is a dataset-release claim, not a code-release claim.

The preprocessing is nontrivial: the paper uses element-centric snippet extraction with stopping conditions based on tree width/depth, marks salient elements with a special target attribute, converts HTML into plaintext sequences, and concatenates action history/instruction/HTML for MiniWoB. Code would matter for reproducing these exact transformations.

The experiments require many implementation details: fine-tuning T5, LaMDA, PaLM, BERT-style models; converting structured web-navigation actions into text; using action-history ablations; and evaluating on specific MiniWoB subsets. The paper describes these at a high level but does not state that training/evaluation scripts are released.

The complete review context supports the point: the reviewer says they examined the supplementary material and “only found the data files,” and under reproducibility repeats that “The Supplementary Material only provides the data file.”

Appendix A.5 is titled “Resource Requirements” but contains no meaningful reproducibility information in the provided paper text, further supporting that implementation/reproduction details are limited.
analysis.reasoning: This weakness is reliable because it directly targets an actual reproducibility gap in the paper. The paper’s conclusions depend on complex empirical pipelines: dataset construction from CommonCrawl, snippet extraction, HTML un-parsing, model-specific fine-tuning, action formatting for MiniWoB, and comparisons against several baselines. Although the paper describes these components, it does not claim to release code, and the review notes that the supplementary material contains only data files. In such a setting, asking for code is not a generic or invented complaint: exact reproduction would require access to preprocessing scripts, training configurations, evaluation scripts, and model-output formatting logic. The paper’s own stated release plan centers on the dataset, not the full experimental codebase. Therefore the segment is grounded in the paper’s scope and limitations.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness saying that code should be released for reproducibility is reliable when the paper’s results depend on nontrivial experimental pipelines, preprocessing, training/evaluation procedures, or model-specific implementation choices, and the paper/supplement only releases data or gives high-level descriptions rather than code. It is especially reliable for empirical papers making comparative performance claims across tasks/models where exact preprocessing, splits, prompts, action formats, or evaluation scripts could materially affect results. It would be less reliable if the paper already clearly released complete runnable code and configurations, or if the result were purely theoretical and not code-dependent.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Check whether the paper actually claims to release code; if it does, a generic “no code” complaint may be unreliable unless the released code is incomplete or inaccessible.
Distinguish dataset release from code release: providing data alone may not be enough to reproduce complex experiments.
Look for nontrivial preprocessing or evaluation details—these strengthen the reliability of a code-reproducibility weakness.
Be cautious if the reviewer asserts they inspected supplementary material; verify whether the paper text or review context supports that claim.
For empirical LLM papers using proprietary or large-scale models, missing code/configuration can be a legitimate reproducibility concern even if full model weights are unavailable.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: However, the lack of technical novelty & contribution makes this work slightly below the acceptance bar of the conference.

analysis.core_claim: The weakness is reliable because the paper’s contribution is mainly an empirical study of applying existing pretrained/fine-tuned LLMs to HTML understanding tasks, rather than a new model, learning algorithm, training objective, or technically novel method. The paper does have contributions, but they are primarily benchmarking, dataset creation, and analysis contributions, so the reviewer’s phrasing about limited technical novelty is grounded in the paper.
paper_evidence: The paper’s stated goal is to investigate whether existing LLMs can be applied to HTML understanding: “we investigate whether LLMs can be applied to HTML understanding to produce better-performing, more sample-efficient HTML understanding models and without the need for custom NN architecture design.”
The method is explicitly the standard pretrained-then-finetuned LLM paradigm: the paper evaluates T5, LaMDA, PaLM, BERT, MobileBERT, and ALBERT variants fine-tuned on three tasks.

The paper emphasizes avoiding specialized architecture design rather than proposing a new architecture: “we take a minimalist approach, providing HTML in raw text form and using widely-adopted transformer networks.”

The technical processing is limited: HTML is converted to plaintext token sequences, with a heuristic snippet extraction step for long pages. This is useful engineering, but not a major new modeling technique.

The main claimed contributions are empirical: evaluating three HTML understanding tasks, comparing architectures/model sizes/pretraining regimes, showing sample efficiency, and creating an auto-labeled CommonCrawl-derived dataset for description generation.
The conclusion frames the findings as practical empirical observations: pretraining is critical, T5 performs best, model size has diminishing returns, and context length is a bottleneck.

The review context is consistent: earlier review lines praise the paper’s writing, experiments, and dataset, but identify the weakness as “primarily empirical” novelty and “standard pretrain-finetune paradigm.” The target sentence summarizes that same criticism.
analysis.reasoning: The target segment should be treated as reliable because it accurately characterizes the nature of the paper’s contribution. The paper does not present a new HTML-specific neural architecture, a new LLM pretraining objective, a new decoding algorithm, or a substantial technical method. Instead, it applies existing LLM architectures to raw HTML inputs, fine-tunes them on selected tasks, and compares performance across models and data regimes. That is a valid empirical contribution, and the reviewer acknowledges this elsewhere as a strength. However, for a conference that expects methodological novelty, it is reasonable and grounded to say the work may fall below the acceptance bar due to limited technical novelty. The only caveat is that the phrase “lack of technical novelty & contribution” could be read too broadly: the paper clearly has contributions in datasets, benchmarking, and empirical analysis. But in the full review context, the reviewer specifically means lack of technical/methodological contribution, which is supported by the paper.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness claiming “limited technical novelty” is reliable when the paper’s own method section mainly uses existing models, standard training/fine-tuning procedures, known objectives, and routine preprocessing, while the claimed contributions are datasets, benchmarks, comparisons, ablations, or empirical findings. Such a weakness remains reliable even if the paper has useful empirical or resource contributions, as long as the review does not deny those contributions and is specifically criticizing the absence of new technical methodology.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark this type of weakness reliable if the paper actually introduces a new architecture, algorithm, training objective, theoretical result, or substantially novel inference procedure that the reviewer ignores.

Be careful with broad wording like “lack of contribution”: if the paper has major dataset or benchmark contributions, the reliable version should be interpreted as “lack of technical/methodological contribution,” not “no contribution at all.”
A novelty criticism is stronger when the paper itself says it uses off-the-shelf models, standard fine-tuning, or avoids custom architecture design.
A novelty criticism is weaker if the reviewer provides no connection to the method, or if the paper’s main novelty is explicitly methodological and central to the results.
Subjective statements about being “below the acceptance bar” can still be reliable if they are tied to a concrete, paper-grounded weakness such as limited technical novelty.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: The modeling part lacks novelty, just basic pre-training + fine-tuning on LLMs, and seems there's no model design based on the features of HTML?

analysis.core_claim: The reviewer’s weakness is grounded: the paper’s modeling contribution is primarily an empirical application of existing pretrained LLM architectures via fine-tuning, rather than a novel HTML-specific model architecture or modeling mechanism.
paper_evidence: The introduction explicitly frames the approach as avoiding custom architecture design: the paper asks whether pretrained LLMs can be applied to HTML understanding “without the need for custom NN architecture design.”

The related work section contrasts prior HTML models that use specialized architectures or HTML preprocessing with this paper’s “minimalist approach,” using raw-text HTML and “widely-adopted transformer networks.”
Section 7, Model Training, lists standard existing models: T5, LaMDA, PaLM, BERT, MobileBERT, and ALBERT. The paper fine-tunes them for the three tasks rather than proposing a new architecture.

For encoder-decoder and decoder-only models, the paper represents inputs and outputs as text: raw HTML snippets/pages in, and text categories/descriptions/actions out. This is standard sequence-to-sequence or decoder-only fine-tuning.
For encoder-only models, the only architectural change described is adding a classification layer after the final encoder layer, which is a standard fine-tuning setup.

The paper’s main experimental analyses are comparisons across architecture families, model sizes, pretraining regimes, data sizes, and action history; these are empirical studies of existing models rather than new model-design contributions.

The paper repeatedly emphasizes findings such as T5 performing best, pretraining improving sample efficiency, and larger models having diminishing returns. These are useful empirical findings, but they do not constitute a new HTML-aware model architecture.

The only HTML-specific mechanisms are input/data handling choices, such as snippet extraction around a salient element, marking the target element with a special attribute, and including action history for MiniWoB. These are preprocessing or input-format choices, not new model designs based on HTML structure.
analysis.reasoning: The target weakness says the modeling part lacks novelty because it is mostly basic pretraining plus fine-tuning on LLMs, with no model design based on HTML features. This matches the paper’s own scope. The paper’s central methodological move is to feed raw or lightly processed HTML into existing LLMs and fine-tune them on HTML-related tasks. It does not introduce a new tree-aware Transformer, DOM-specific attention mechanism, hierarchical encoder, rendering-aware representation, or HTML-structured inductive bias. In fact, the authors present the absence of specialized architecture as part of their contribution: they show that off-the-shelf LLMs can transfer well to HTML understanding. Therefore, the reviewer’s concern is not a misreading; it is a valid assessment of the modeling novelty. The only caveat is that the paper does have HTML-specific preprocessing, such as snippet extraction using the HTML tree and target marking, and MiniWoB action-history conditioning. However, those do not undermine the reviewer’s point because they are not new model architectures or substantial HTML-aware model designs. The weakness is also consistent with the rest of the review, which acknowledges the paper’s empirical value while questioning whether the modeling contribution is too standard.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness claiming “limited modeling novelty” is reliable when the paper mainly applies existing pretrained architectures with standard fine-tuning/prompting/input formatting, and the paper’s contributions are empirical comparisons, datasets, or benchmarks rather than new architectural mechanisms. Check the model/training section: if it names off-the-shelf models, uses standard text-in/text-out or classification-head fine-tuning, and any domain-specific steps are preprocessing or serialization rather than new model components, then the criticism is grounded—even if the paper intentionally frames this simplicity as a strength.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark this kind of weakness reliable if the paper actually proposes a substantive new model component, such as DOM-aware attention, tree-structured encoding, rendering/layout fusion, custom pretraining objective, or an HTML-specific architecture, and the reviewer ignores it.
Distinguish model novelty from dataset/task novelty: a paper can be novel empirically or benchmark-wise while still having low modeling novelty.
Preprocessing is not usually enough to refute a lack-of-modeling-novelty criticism unless the preprocessing is itself a central learned modeling mechanism.

If the paper explicitly claims novelty only in evaluation, dataset creation, or demonstrating transfer, then a reviewer can reasonably criticize the absence of new modeling even if the paper’s results are strong.

Be careful with absolute wording like “just fine-tuning” if the paper also includes nontrivial RL, new objectives, or substantial adaptation methods; here, the wording remains acceptable because the core modeling is standard fine-tuning of existing LLMs.

paper_title: UNDERSTANDING HTML WITH LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
segment_text: My main concern is that the new task is not clearly justified, and the modeling part might be too standard -- there is no HTML-specific model design involved, just studying basic LLMs.

analysis.core_claim: The weakness is reliable because it accurately reflects two paper-grounded issues: (1) the newly proposed Description Generation benchmark is introduced and evaluated with limited justification beyond a plausible motivation and dataset construction procedure, and (2) the modeling contribution is intentionally standard LLM fine-tuning rather than a new HTML-specific architecture.
paper_evidence: The paper’s own framing emphasizes applying existing LLMs to HTML rather than designing a new model: it says it uses “off-the-shelf LLM” style transfer and aims to avoid “custom NN architecture design.”

In Related Work, the authors explicitly contrast their approach with specialized HTML architectures and say: “our work takes a minimalist approach, providing HTML in raw text form and using widely-adopted transformer networks.” This supports the reviewer’s claim that there is no HTML-specific model design.

The Model Training section lists standard pretrained architectures—T5, LaMDA, PaLM, BERT, MobileBERT, ALBERT—and describes fine-tuning them with text input/text output or a standard classification head. There is no new architecture, loss, HTML-aware attention, DOM-specific module, or training objective introduced.

The main HTML-specific processing is snippet extraction around a salient element and marking that element with a special target attribute. This is preprocessing rather than model design, so it does not invalidate the reviewer’s criticism that the modeling is basic LLM fine-tuning.

For the new Description Generation task, the paper motivates it briefly as locating textual descriptions associated with an element, useful for accessibility/browser control. But the justification is relatively thin: the paper does not deeply analyze why this benchmark captures substantially different capabilities from semantic classification or web navigation.

The Description Generation dataset is auto-labeled using the HTML label element’s for attribute, then modified to avoid trivial cheating by replacing label tags and removing examples with only one text span. This is a reasonable construction, but it also means the task is essentially extractive label recovery from HTML snippets, which makes the reviewer’s request for more justification plausible.

The results for Description Generation are brief: Table 3 reports very high exact-match accuracy for pretrained models, around or above 90%, with BLEU/ROUGE also high. The paper gives limited error analysis or task-difficulty analysis for this new benchmark compared with the more extensive discussion of semantic classification and MiniWoB.

The review context shows the reviewer is not dismissing the whole paper: they acknowledge “solid empirical contributions,” “a novel and interesting task,” and useful studies of architecture/scaling/context. The target segment is a focused novelty/justification concern, consistent with the paper’s scope.
analysis.reasoning: The target segment is grounded in the paper rather than being an unsupported complaint. The authors’ central methodological choice is to evaluate existing LLM families on HTML tasks using raw/unparsed HTML plus limited preprocessing. That is scientifically useful as an empirical study, but it also means the modeling novelty is low. The paper itself repeatedly presents this as a virtue—showing that pretrained LLMs can work without specialized architectures—so the reviewer’s statement that the modeling is “too standard” and lacks “HTML-specific model design” is factually aligned with the paper. Similarly, the new Description Generation task is real and reasonably motivated, but the paper’s justification is comparatively brief: it explains the accessibility/browser-control motivation and the CommonCrawl auto-labeling method, then reports high performance with limited deeper analysis of what unique capability the task measures. Given that semantic classification and description generation both involve associating an HTML element with surrounding semantic text, it is reasonable for the reviewer to ask for clearer differentiation and value of the benchmark. The weakness should therefore be considered reliable, even though it is partly evaluative: it fairly identifies a limitation in novelty and benchmark justification based on the paper’s actual claims and experimental design.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness is reliable when it identifies a limitation that follows directly from the paper’s own stated scope and methods, even if the limitation is partly subjective. For example, if a paper’s contribution is mainly benchmarking existing pretrained models with standard fine-tuning, and the paper explicitly says it avoids specialized architecture design, then a criticism that the modeling lacks novelty or HTML/task-specific design is grounded. Likewise, if a new benchmark is introduced with only brief motivation, limited analysis of what distinct capability it measures, and very high baseline/model performance, then a criticism that the task needs stronger justification is reliable. Do not mark such a weakness unreliable merely because the authors intentionally chose a simple method; intentional simplicity can still be a valid novelty concern.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Check whether the reviewer’s “lack of novelty” criticism contradicts or matches the paper’s actual method. Here it matches: the paper uses standard T5/PaLM/LaMDA/BERT fine-tuning.
Distinguish between model design and preprocessing. Snippet extraction or target marking may be HTML-specific preprocessing, but it is not the same as a novel HTML-aware model architecture.

For benchmark-justification criticisms, look for whether the paper explains what new capability the task measures, provides strong baselines, analyzes difficulty/errors, and differentiates it from existing tasks. If these are thin, the criticism is likely reliable.
A weakness can be reliable even when the paper has valid empirical contributions; reliability means the concern is grounded, not that it is decisive for rejection.
Be cautious if a review claims “no contribution” when the paper has datasets/experiments; but a narrower claim like “modeling is standard” may still be accurate.

paper_title: Learning Entailment-Based Sentence Embeddings from Natural Language Inference

review_score.Experience Assessment: I have published in this field for several years.

segment_text: However, the question becomes, how many fewer parameters are being learned to accept a performance that is in the same ball park but that does not exceed the SOTA.

analysis.core_claim: The reviewer’s weakness is that the paper argues for accepting somewhat lower/roughly comparable NLI performance in exchange for fewer learned parameters, but does not clearly quantify the parameter reduction or show state-of-the-art-level performance, making the tradeoff hard to judge.
paper_evidence: The paper explicitly motivates the method as a parameter-free interaction layer: “we propose a parameter-free interaction layer consisting of only a few scores,” replacing the common MLP interaction layer.
The abstract claims the parameter-free model achieves “results on natural language inference competitive with MLP-based models,” not that it surpasses state of the art.

Section 1.2 emphasizes parameter reduction: the MLP can require many parameters, e.g. “800k of the total 2.1m model parameters” in a cited Dynamic Self-Attention model, while the proposed interaction layer has no parameters apart from the final classifier.

The paper’s own results acknowledge a performance gap: for single-sentence encoders, “our interaction model performs slightly worse than the MLP-based model,” and with BERT/SBERT, “We see a small decrease in accuracies for both SNLI and MNLI for our much simpler interaction model.”

The paper frames the benefit as being close/competitive plus better transfer/generalization, rather than exceeding SOTA: “this simple interaction layer is empirically competitive with MLP-based models” and “the resulting sentence embeddings… transfer better.”

Although the paper discusses parameter reduction qualitatively and gives some contextual numbers for an MLP in prior work, it does not present a clear table comparing the total number of learned parameters for each experimental model against its accuracy, which is what the reviewer is asking for.
analysis.reasoning:
The target segment is grounded in the paper. The reviewer is not inventing a flaw: the central bargain of the paper is indeed that a parameter-free, interpretable interaction function can perform in the same general range as MLP-based interaction models, while using fewer trainable parameters and potentially transferring better. The paper repeatedly describes its results as “competitive,” and its own discussion concedes lower in-domain accuracy in several settings. Thus the reviewer’s phrase “same ball park but does not exceed the SOTA” is a fair characterization of the paper’s in-domain empirical positioning, even if the paper’s main claim is not strictly to beat SOTA.

The reviewer’s question about “how many fewer parameters” is also reasonable. The paper states that the proposed interaction layer is parameter-free and contrasts it with MLP interaction layers that can contain many parameters, but it does not provide a systematic parameter-count/accuracy tradeoff analysis for the reported models. Since the claimed advantage partly depends on parameter economy, a reviewer can reliably ask whether the reduction is large enough to justify accepting slightly lower or merely comparable performance. The paper’s transfer results may partially answer a different concern—generalization—but they do not eliminate the need to quantify the parameter-performance tradeoff.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness is reliable when it targets a tradeoff that the paper itself makes central—e.g., fewer parameters, more interpretability, or efficiency in exchange for comparable but not superior accuracy—and the paper does not quantify that tradeoff clearly enough in its experiments. If the paper claims “competitive” rather than SOTA performance, reports results that are sometimes below baselines, and motivates the method by reduced parameterization without a systematic parameter-count comparison, then a reviewer’s request to justify ‘how many fewer parameters for how much performance loss’ is grounded and should be treated as reliable.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark such a criticism unreliable merely because the proposed method has another benefit, such as transfer performance or interpretability; the criticism can still be valid if parameter reduction is part of the paper’s motivation.

Check whether the paper actually includes total parameter counts or only qualitative statements like “parameter-free interaction layer.” Absence of a full parameter/accuracy table supports the reliability of this weakness.

Distinguish between criticizing lack of SOTA and demanding SOTA. Here the reviewer’s point is not simply “not SOTA is bad,” but that the paper should justify the practical tradeoff between reduced parameters and non-superior performance.
If a paper’s experiments already contain a detailed efficiency-vs-accuracy analysis, this kind of weakness would be less reliable. In this case, they do not.

paper_title: Learning Entailment-Based Sentence Embeddings from Natural Language Inference

review_score.Experience Assessment: I have published in this field for several years.

segment_text: However, I do have some concerns about their claims that this helps in transfer learning to other NLI tasks.

analysis.core_claim: The reviewer’s concern that the paper’s claim of improved transfer to other NLI tasks is not fully convincing is grounded in the paper: transfer generalization is a central claimed contribution, but the evidence is mixed and depends on discounting some datasets and averaging across heterogeneous benchmarks.
paper_evidence: The paper explicitly claims transfer benefits multiple times: the abstract says the inductive bias “leads to better generalisation to other related datasets,” and the introduction/overview says the embeddings “transfer better to different NLI datasets.”

Section 4 is dedicated to “Evaluation of Transfer Performance,” motivated by the claim that the parameter-free entailment/contradiction interaction layer should learn more general entailment regularities rather than dataset artifacts.
In Section 4.4, the authors train models on MNLI and evaluate on 11 other NLI or NLI-like datasets, comparing their proposed SBERT model against an HM+SBERT baseline.

The paper itself acknowledges mixed results: “our proposed model performs better than the baseline on 5 datasets, the same on one, and worse on 3,” while excluding or downplaying SNLI and ADD-ONE-RTE from the main qualitative comparison.

Table 4, as described in the text, is used to support a “substantial improvement in generalisation,” but the authors also note that SNLI has similar annotation biases to MNLI and that ADD-ONE-RTE is essentially failed by both models, making parts of the transfer evidence difficult to interpret.

The reviewer’s broader review context accurately summarizes that the model performs competitively in-domain but raises doubts specifically about whether the transfer experiments justify the stronger generalization claim.
analysis.reasoning: The target segment is reliable because it identifies a real pressure point in the paper’s argument. The paper does not merely present transfer as an incidental experiment; it frames better transfer to other NLI datasets as a key motivation and contribution. Therefore, questioning the strength of this evidence is within scope. The transfer section provides some positive evidence, but it is not uniformly positive: the proposed model wins on some datasets, ties on one, and loses on several, with the authors asking readers to discount certain cases due to shared biases or failed generalization. That makes the reviewer’s concern reasonable and grounded rather than speculative. Even if the reviewer’s next sentence may somewhat overstate the situation by saying the approach transfers “more poorly” overall, the selected target sentence itself is more general: it says the reviewer has concerns about the transfer-learning claim. Given the mixed table-level results and the paper’s strong wording about better generalization, that concern is justified.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness is reliable when it challenges a paper’s claimed generalization or transfer benefit and the paper’s own evidence is mixed, selectively interpreted, averaged over heterogeneous datasets, or dependent on excluding/downweighting inconvenient cases. If transfer/generalization is a stated contribution, reviewers may legitimately flag insufficient or unconvincing transfer evidence even when some individual results support the claim.
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Check whether the criticized claim is actually made by the paper; here, better transfer/generalization is explicitly claimed in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Check whether the empirical evidence is uniformly supportive or mixed; here, the model improves on some transfer datasets but underperforms on others.
Check whether the authors rely on post hoc explanations to discount negative results, such as shared annotation biases or both models failing on a dataset.
Check whether the reviewer’s concern is proportional. A broad concern about convincingness is reliable even if a later stronger statement in the review may overgeneralize the results.
Check whether the requested additional analysis, such as error analysis or probing of embeddings, follows naturally from ambiguity in the reported results.

paper_title: Learning Entailment-Based Sentence Embeddings from Natural Language Inference

review_score.Experience Assessment: I have published in this field for several years.

segment_text: Two datasets that they do worse on they try to discount for either having terrible, below random performance (which is true) and the other for having the same biases as MNLI.

analysis.core_claim: The reviewer’s weakness is grounded: in the transfer-results discussion, the paper explicitly sets aside two underperforming transfer datasets—SNLI and ADD-ONE-RTE—by arguing that SNLI shares MNLI annotation biases and that ADD-ONE-RTE is essentially failed by both models, making the comparison less meaningful.
paper_evidence: In Section 4.4, the paper evaluates transfer from MNLI-trained models to 11 NLI-related datasets and compares the proposed entailment-score SBERT model against the heuristic-matching SBERT baseline.

The paper explicitly says: “As shown in prior work (Belinkov et al., 2019a), the SNLI dataset has very similar annotation biases to the MNLI data which the models were trained on, so we do not expect any improvement in the relative performance of the two models for SNLI.” This matches the reviewer’s claim about discounting one dataset because it has the same biases as MNLI.

The paper also says: “Also, for the ADD-ONE-RTE dataset, both models essentially fail to generalise to this data, so the comparison is not very meaningful.” This matches the reviewer’s claim about discounting another dataset because performance is terrible / not meaningful.

After excluding or downplaying those cases, the paper summarizes: “For the remaining datasets, our proposed model performs better than the baseline on 5 datasets, the same on one, and worse on 3.” This supports the reviewer’s concern that the authors’ positive transfer conclusion depends partly on how these problematic datasets are treated.

The broader review context is also consistent: the reviewer’s main concern is that the transfer experiments are not convincing, especially because the proposed model’s advantage is task-dependent and some worse-performing cases are explained away rather than analyzed.
analysis.reasoning: The target segment is not inventing a limitation; it directly reflects the paper’s own transfer-results discussion. The two datasets are identifiable from the paper: SNLI is discounted because it shares annotation biases with MNLI, and ADD-ONE-RTE is discounted because both models fail to generalize, making the comparison ‘not very meaningful.’ The reviewer’s wording ‘try to discount’ is evaluative, but the underlying factual claim is accurate: the authors explicitly provide reasons not to treat those datasets as strong evidence against their method. This is a reliable weakness because it points to a real interpretive issue in the paper’s evidence for better transfer: the claimed average/generalization improvement is partly supported after carving out datasets where the proposed model does not clearly help. The segment is especially grounded because it uses the authors’ own stated caveats, rather than speculating about unreported experiments.
analysis.reusable_baseline_rule: A review weakness is reliable when it criticizes how a paper interprets or discounts experimental results and the paper text actually contains those caveats, exclusions, or post-hoc explanations. Check whether the named datasets/settings are present in the experiments, whether the paper reports weaker results there, and whether the authors explicitly argue those cases are less meaningful due to factors like dataset bias, failed generalization, or non-comparability. If all three are true, the weakness should be treated as grounded even if the reviewer uses mildly evaluative language such as ‘discount’ or ‘explain away.’
warning_signs_for_future_reviews: Do not mark such a criticism unreliable merely because the reviewer’s wording is somewhat opinionated; verify whether the paper itself makes the disputed caveats.
Be cautious if the reviewer claims the authors ignored or discounted results but the paper actually gives a balanced quantitative analysis including those cases.
Check whether the allegedly discounted datasets are genuinely underperforming cases for the proposed method; if the table shows the method wins there, the criticism may be unreliable.
Check whether the paper’s reason for excluding a dataset was pre-specified or methodological rather than post-hoc; that would weaken the review criticism.
For transfer-learning claims, pay close attention to whether averages or summary counts depend on excluding datasets with poor or anomalous performance.

paper_title: Learning Entailment-Based Sentence Embeddings from Natural Language Inference

The paper’s conclusion nevertheless summarizes the transfer finding positively, saying the inductive bias leads to better generalization to other NLI datasets.

The review context correctly identifies that the paper’s transfer evidence is mixed and that performance differs substantially across target datasets, making the general transfer claim less straightforward than the paper’s summary suggests.
